news.2026-11-09-chine-prix-usines-5-7-po: China: factory-gate prices rise 5.7%, the most since June 2022, while consumer prices slow

Chinese wholesale prices rose 5.7% year on year in October, their fastest pace since June 2022, while consumer inflation slowed to 0.7%. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, more expensive imported energy is pushing up factory prices while food prices fall [1][2].

Chinese factories make a large share of the electronics, clothing and parts you buy. When their costs rise, the increase can, with a delay, show up in export prices and therefore on European shelves, especially if energy stays expensive. Conversely, almost flat consumer prices in China say that its households spend little: that is what pushes the country to sell more abroad.

On 9 November the National Bureau of Statistics published October's producer price index (PPI, the price of goods leaving the factory): +5.7% year on year, against +5.0% in September and +5.3% expected by economists polled by Reuters [1][2].
It is the third acceleration in a row, and the fastest pace since June 2022 [2][3].
On the consumer side, inflation (CPI) slowed to +0.7% year on year, against +0.9% in September and +0.8% expected; month on month, prices were flat [2][4].
Underlying inflation, which excludes food and energy, fell to +0.8% from +1.0% in September, below the +0.9% expected [2][4].
Food prices fell 2.9% year on year, a 13-month low: this sharper-than-expected drop offsets higher gasoline prices [2][4].
Over the first ten months of 2026, consumer prices are up just 0.9% from the same period of 2025 [5].
Dong Lijuan, the Bureau's chief statistician, attributes the rise in factory prices to higher international energy prices and greater demand for coal and gas for power generation and heating [1].

Key point: in China it is factories, not households, that are seeing their costs climb, and this 5-point gap between wholesale prices (+5.7%) and retail prices (+0.7%) is putting companies under pressure [2][4].

The mechanism is simple: a manufacturer that pays more for energy and raw materials but sells to customers who spend little cannot raise its prices, and its margin shrinks. Analysts quoted in the press speak of squeezed margins and weak domestic demand [2][4]. CNBC sees a delicate balancing act for the authorities, between supporting consumption and containing costs [2].

The shock comes from energy: the SCMP links the highest PPI since 2022 to the war in Iran, and CNBC was already describing, in May and then June, wholesale inflation close to a four-year high because of the cost of imported raw materials [3][6][7].

The rise comes as China exports at full speed: in September its exports had jumped 36.3% year on year and its trade surplus reached $938 billion, according to Fortune, which notes that pressure is mounting for it to rebalance its trade with Europe [8]. If wholesale prices stay high, they partly end up in the price of exported goods.

news.2026-11-09-canada-etats-unis-concep: Canada–US: Trump talks of a "concept" of a deal that would include the Keystone XL pipeline, but Ottawa says "not quite" and the 50% tariffs remain

Donald Trump says he and Mark Carney have "the concept" of a trade deal, with the building of the Keystone XL pipeline and zero tariffs for American farmers. The Canadian prime minister speaks of a constructive exchange, but there is no text and no rate, and the 50% tariffs remain in force [1][2][3].

If the deal with Washington is reached, Canada will be less pressed to turn to other markets; if it fails, it will try harder to sell elsewhere, including in Europe, which can influence prices and trade agreements. The protection of French, cited by Mark Carney as a red line, directly concerns French speakers.

Donald Trump said he and Mark Carney had "the concept" of a deal and that building the Keystone XL pipeline would be part of it; the AP agency reported his remarks on 1 November, two days before the US midterm elections [1][2].
He added: "Part of the agreement is that our farmers will have to pay no tariffs," while implying that the details were not settled [2].

Mark Carney described a constructive conversation with Trump and said negotiators would work toward a deal in the coming weeks; he had also said a deal before the 3 November vote was not on the cards [1][3].
Ottawa mainly wants relief from US sectoral tariffs on cars, steel, aluminium and wood products [3].
The figures differ between outlets: The Auto Wire says a 50% duty tied to Canada's car duties remains in force, and also mentions a threatened 25% duty on 1 January on vehicles built in Canada [2].

The talks restart after August's failure: Mark Carney had said Washington "asked too much and offered too little", then the United States imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian goods, and Canada retaliated on about $20 billion of American goods [4][5][6].
Key point: a "concept" is not a deal. The text, the rates and the timetable do not exist yet, and the two sides do not describe the same thing, which makes any announcement premature [2].

The stakes are heavy for Canada: the United States takes 72% of its goods exports, and exports to its neighbour fell 6.6% in July, according to Statistics Canada [7]. Every week without a deal weighs on steel, aluminium and car plants.

The issue is also political on both sides. Tariffs have become a campaign issue in states where Republicans cannot afford to lose, such as Michigan and Maine, according to Al Jazeera [8]. On the Canadian side, Mark Carney explained in August that he had rejected demands that threatened the country's sovereignty, the protection of French and the car industry [2][4].

Another blurry point: Keystone XL, the pipeline cited by Trump, and the exemption for American farmers do not appear in the grounds of the 20 July US proclamation, which rests on vehicles, which suggests these elements would have to be written into a future text [2].

news.2026-11-09-chine-japon-un-an-apres-: China–Japan: a year after Takaichi's words on Taiwan, relations remain frozen, from rare earths to seafood, and everything hinges on Shenzhen on 18 November

On 7 November 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger a military response from Tokyo. A year later, Beijing keeps its sanctions (seafood, rare earths, tourism), and Japan hopes for at least a handshake at the APEC summit [1][2][3].

If you own an electric car or a device with a magnet (headphones, hard drive, wind turbine), you depend on these rare earths. This quarrel shows how a diplomatic conflict can, within weeks, block manufacturing chains worldwide, and why Europe is also trying to reduce its dependence on China.

On 7 November 2025, before Parliament, Sanae Takaichi said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could lead to a Japanese military response; a spokesman for China's Commerce Ministry called her remarks "openly erroneous" and said they had "fundamentally undermined the political foundation" of relations [2][3].

Beijing reimposed its ban on Japanese seafood in November 2025, citing promised documents that Tokyo had allegedly not provided and the anger of Chinese public opinion; China accounted for less than 2% of Japan's seafood exports last year, against 22.5% in 2022 [2][4].
On 6 January 2026, China restricted exports of dual-use goods to Japan, including rare earths and permanent magnets; Japan depended on China for 63% of its rare-earth imports in 2024 [5][6].
Nissan and Suzuki reported supply disruptions because of these restrictions [6].

Beijing also advised its citizens against travelling to Japan and had Japanese animated films and concerts cancelled; CSIS judges the effect on tourism limited, because visitors from Taiwan, South Korea, the United States and Hong Kong offset the drop in Chinese arrivals [1][6].
Takaichi says she wants "constructive" ties with China, but Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara declined to say whether the remarks would be withdrawn, which Beijing demands [1].

In late September, former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya met China's top diplomat and top economic official, the first contacts at that level between a Japanese politician and Beijing since the affair [2].
Key point: this is not a mere diplomatic disagreement, it is lasting economic pressure between two neighbours whose companies depend on each other [1][5].

The most effective weapon is rare earths: without permanent magnets you cannot make electric-car motors or many electronic devices. The restrictions first hit the Japanese car industry, and Japan is trying to reduce its dependence, which one analysis puts at around 65% today against 90% in 2010, a figure not confirmed by the other sources [1][6].
Beijing thus seeks a retraction that Tokyo refuses to give: accepting would mean, in Tokyo's eyes, giving up saying what Japan would do if Taiwan were attacked [1][2].

The next test is the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November: Tokyo is pressing to obtain at least a standard handshake for Takaichi, a gesture that would serve as a signal of a possible thaw [1][7].

news.2026-11-09-argentine-croissance-0-7: Argentina: economists now see only 0.7% growth in 2026 and a 2.3% contraction in the third quarter, three days before the inflation figure

The central bank's monthly survey (REM), published on 5 November, cuts Argentina's 2026 growth from 1.5% to 0.7% and expects inflation of 1.8% in October. INDEC publishes the official figure on Thursday 12 November, in a country where the strong peso is slowing activity [1][2][3][5].

If you travel to or invest in Argentina, the strong peso makes the country expensive for visitors, which partly explains the contraction in activity. For a European reader, this case shows that very high inflation can be calmed, but that an artificially high exchange rate has a growth cost. This is information, never investment advice.
The Central Bank of Argentina's Market Expectations Survey (REM), published on 5 November, lowers expected 2026 growth to 0.7%, from 1.5% in the previous edition [1][2][3].
According to the same survey, activity contracted by 2.3% in the third quarter, with a 2% rebound in the fourth [2].
Economists expect inflation of 1.8% in October (core inflation: 1.7%) and 30.4% over the whole of 2026; the wholesale dollar would stand at 1,590 pesos in December [1][2].
The official October figure will be published by INDEC on Thursday 12 November; the consultants polled expect 1.8% to 2.1% [5].
In September, prices rose 1.9% over one month, after 1.7% in August, giving 33.4% over twelve months [7].
Economy Minister Luis Caputo rejects this diagnosis: he considers the seasonally adjusted series too volatile and points to a trend indicator showing 29 months of growth [6].

Key point: Argentina has slowed inflation, but at the price of activity. A strong peso makes imports cheap and curbs prices, but penalises producers, exporters and tourism, as Bloomberg's analysis puts it [4][6].

The fall in expected growth (from 1.5% to 0.7% in one month) is the clearest signal: economists are revising this figure down, and the negative third-quarter figure means the economy would have contracted in the middle of the year; the REM expects a 2% rebound in the fourth [2][3].

The debate is also a quarrel over figures: Minister Luis Caputo challenges the seasonally adjusted series, which he considers too volatile, and counters with a trend indicator showing 29 months of growth [6]. What each curve measures is not the same thing, and the 12 November inflation figure will also arbitrate on the solidity of disinflation.

news.2026-11-09-etats-unis-democrates-ab: United States: Democrats, now in control of Congress, want to repeal Trump's tariffs, but he promises a veto and they lack the votes to override it

After their victory in the midterm elections, Democrats want to use their majorities to undo Donald Trump's tariffs, starting with those on Canada. But the president promises to use his veto, and without Republican votes they lack the two-thirds needed [1][2][3].

These tariffs raise the price of imported goods in the United States and weigh on European exporters (wine, machinery, luxury goods). If Congress manages to reduce them, it will be good news for them; if it fails, they will have to live with lasting uncertainty. For markets, it is one more factor to watch besides the Fed and inflation.

Democrats have taken Congress: The Hill cites projections of 262 House members and 55 senators, while the analysis centre The Center Square speaks of at least 54 senators and a House majority with dozens of races still undecided [1][3].

Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, has made ending the tariffs one of his priorities; the idea is to quickly vote a bill that gives Congress back its power over trade, then to go after the 50% duties on Canadian goods [1][2][4].
Before the vote, Ken Martin, chair of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), had said: "The first thing they should do is repeal the tariffs that Donald Trump put in place" [8].

Donald Trump replies: "I have the ultimate power, it's called veto"; to override it, 67 votes would be needed in the Senate and 290 in the House, which Democrats do not have without Republicans [3][4].
Precedent: the House passed by 219 votes to 211, with six Republicans, a resolution ending the emergency that justified the Canada tariffs, without reaching two-thirds [5][2].

Legal framework: the Supreme Court ruled on 20 February 2026 that the IEEPA law does not authorise tariffs; the temporary 10% surcharge (Section 122) expired on 23 July and was replaced by 10% to 12.5% duties (Section 301) on 60 countries and territories, with no end date [6][7].
An independent estimate puts the cost of repealing the remaining tariffs at about $85.5 billion a year, which matters for the deficit [3].

Key point: the 3 November result changes the balance of power, but is not enough to change trade policy, because the Constitution gives the president the veto and two-thirds of both chambers are needed to override it [3][4].

Democrats are therefore considering several routes: targeted bills (for example on Canada) that can win over Republicans, limits attached to budgets that Congress must pass, and hearings to examine the tariffs; Ron Wyden, the future chair of the Senate Finance Committee, wants to use it to reassert Congress's power over trade [4].

The courts remain the most likely route in the short term, as the Supreme Court's February decision showed, then the legal battle over Section 122 before the Court of International Trade, whose May decision is suspended on appeal [3][6][9].

For Washington's partners, Canada, Mexico, China, Europe, the question is simple: whether the current tariffs are lasting. For now they are, at least until the new Congress takes office in January 2027 [2][7].

news.2026-11-09-inde-inflation-octobre-6: India: October inflation could come close to or exceed 6%, the central bank's ceiling, a month after its first rate hike since 2023

A Reuters poll published on 6 November sees Indian inflation in October approaching the top of the Reserve Bank's range (2% to 6%), driven by food. The official figure is out on 12 November, a month after a rate hike to 5.50% [1][2][3].

For a French reader, India is a large market and a supplier of medicines, textiles and IT: stronger inflation and higher rates make credit more expensive there and can slow demand for imported products.
In the Reuters poll, forecasts for October range from 5.50% to 6.60%; food inflation would rise from 7.74% in September to 8.20% [1][2].
ICRA's forecast is 6.1%, a 24-month high and above the central bank's ceiling [4].
BofA Securities expects double-digit inflation on meat, fish, oils and fats, fruit, vegetables and sugar [1].
On 7 October the Reserve Bank raised its policy rate by 25 basis points, from 5.25% to 5.50%, unanimously, a first hike since February 2023 [3].

Key point: rising food prices, linked according to economists to near-drought conditions in several regions and to a base effect tied to the GST cut, are pushing inflation toward the central bank's ceiling [1][2].
An economist at Union Bank of India thinks the bank could continue its "calibrated" progress in steps of 25 basis points; the next meeting is scheduled for 2 to 4 December [1][3].

news.2026-11-09-indonesie-croissance-5-4: Indonesia: growth accelerates to 5.47% in the third quarter, better than expected, and the rupiah is back below 18,100 per dollar

Indonesia's economy grew 5.47% year on year in the third quarter, against 5.29% in the second and 5.18% expected by analysts, according to the BPS institute. Household consumption and industry, boosted by biodiesel, drive growth [1][2][3].
Indonesia sells nickel, used in batteries, and palm oil, found in many food products: its growth and its currency matter for the prices of these commodities.
On 5 November the BPS statistics institute announced +5.47% year on year, against 5.18% expected in the Reuters poll and 5.29% in the second quarter [1][2].
Over one quarter, growth is 1.59%, above the 1.3% expected; over nine months, it reaches 5.45% [2][3].
Household consumption contributes 2.62 points of growth, and industry 1.20 points, with the B50 biodiesel mandate boosting palm-oil processing [3].
The rupiah fell back below 18,100 per dollar on 5 November, after breaking through 17,800 at the end of May [4][5].
Key point: activity is accelerating, and Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara estimates that 2026 growth could reach 5.5%, above the budget target of 5.4% [2][3].
Bank Indonesia held its rate at 5.75% on 21 October, judging the economy resilient [3]. The currency remains fragile: the rupiah was under pressure in 2026, with a record low in early June [4][5].

The Kospi lost 11.71% in five sessions, with foreign investors selling 10,440 billion won of shares. Friday 6 November's 6.02% drop had triggered a trading halt [1][2][3].
Samsung and SK hynix make the memory chips in our phones and computers: if their profits falter, the prices of these components can move. This is information, never investment advice.
On 6 November the Kospi closed down 6.02% at 5,059.69 points; the circuit breaker had been triggered around 9:03 a.m., after a fall of more than 8% at the open [3][4].
SK hynix lost more than 10% and Samsung Electronics 6.35%; foreign ownership of Samsung fell to 45.95%, a 17-year low [4].
Foreign investors sold 10,440 billion won of shares last week [2][4].

The 11 November date is twofold: the release of US inflation and CoreWeave's results, before Seoul opens; the Philadelphia semiconductor index rebounded more than 4% overnight [1].

news.2026-11-09-taiwan-elections-locales: Taiwan: three weeks before the 28 November local elections, Taipei, the city everyone is watching, is decided by a few points

On 28 November, Taiwan votes for all its local tiers: 19,695 candidates for 11,051 posts, a test before the 2028 presidential election. In Taipei, Kuomintang incumbent mayor Chiang Wan-an sees his lead melt against Puma Shen of the Democratic Progressive Party [1][2][3].
Taiwan is at the heart of world chip manufacturing: the stability of its political life interests all makers of computers and phones.
The "nine-in-one" vote elects mayors, councillors and neighbourhood officials at the same time: 19,695 candidates for 11,051 seats [1][4].

In Taipei, TVBS gave Chiang Wan-an a 28-point lead in May and 8 in early October; a United Daily News poll taken from 20 to 25 October puts Puma Shen ahead, 45% to 41%, within the margin of error [3].
In Taichung, a poll commissioned by the KMT, published on 2 November, has Johnny Chiang ahead of Ho Hsin-chun, 38.3% to 28.1%; four of the five October polls put him ahead [2].
KMT chair Cheng Li-wun has launched a series of large rallies, the first in central Taiwan; the Democratic Progressive Party, for its part, urges caution about polls [1].

Key point: these elections serve as a rehearsal before the 2028 presidential election: the map of cities will show whether President Lai Ching-te's Democratic Progressive Party keeps its momentum or whether the Kuomintang regains ground [1][4].

Alliances matter: in Kaohsiung, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim campaigns with Lai, while Ko Wen-je, founder of the Taiwan People's Party, backs the KMT candidate; in New Taipei, the TPP chairman stepped aside for the KMT's Lee Shu-chuan, against Su Chiao-hui; the DPP has held Tainan since 1997 [2][1].
